html:
The Battle of Borodino was fought on 7 September 1812 at the village of Borodino, about 110 km west of Moscow in Russia. Napoleon's army attacked the Russian army of General Kutuzov and took the field, but did not destroy it. It was the bloodiest single day of the Napoleonic Wars.

Napoleon invaded Russia in June 1812 with more than 400,000 men, to force Tsar Alexander I back into his blockade of British trade. The Russians retreated for ten weeks, burning supplies as they went. At last Kutuzov turned to defend Moscow. Each side had roughly 130,000 men. Napoleon chose plain frontal attacks on the Russian earthworks. They changed hands again and again under the fire of over a thousand guns. By evening the French held them, but Napoleon would not send in his Guard to finish the battle. About 70,000 men were killed or wounded, more of them Russian.

Kutuzov slipped away with his army intact and gave up Moscow, which burned. The tsar refused to talk peace. In October Napoleon began to retreat, and cold, hunger and Russian attacks destroyed his army. The next year his enemies united against him at Leipzig.
